I'm looking at this text about the human complement C9 gene, noting it discusses C9 deficiency and its association with recurrent infections like neisserial disease, which I should flag as the disease mention.

The authors studied a Swiss family with inherited C9 deficiency and found two distinct point mutations causing premature stop codons—one in exon 2, one in exon 4—that segregate independently in heterozygous relatives. They also revised the gene's exon-intron boundaries, particularly around exons 4-6 and 10-11.

Now I'm working through which mentions of "C9 deficiency" qualify as a Specific Disease span versus which surrounding modifiers (like "inherited" or "heterozygous") should be excluded from the annotation span, going through each occurrence in the text systematically.

Looking at "the complete deficiency of both the probands," I note that's a bare, unlabeled mention since the of-phrase refers to the probands rather than a molecular target. Then I'm examining the general statement "Deficiency of terminal complement components is generally associated with recurrent neisseria infections" — this is trickier since it's describing a broad class of conditions rather than a case-specific subject, so it may fall under Disease Class or Unqualified generic rather than Specific Disease.

Actually, deficiency-type nominals seem governed by a special subsection that excludes them from the compositional Disease Class rule entirely, so "deficiency of terminal complement components" shouldn't get a compositional label even though Rule B(j) might otherwise suggest broad-class treatment. I'm leaning toward not annotating it as Disease Class after all, given that specific carve-out.

Moving to "recurrent neisseria infections" — the causal-agent premodifier "Neisseria" plus head "infections" forms a Specific Disease via the individuating anchor rule, while "recurrent" functions as a separate timing/course descriptor that sits outside the core disease span.

I then work through the remaining entity decisions in the C9 deficiency passage: "C9 deficiency" instances get Specific Disease labels wherever they appear with "with," "basis of," or "cause of" framing, while bare terms like "deficiency," "mutations," and gene/protein descriptions stay unlabeled per the standard exclusion rules. I settle on including "Deficiency of terminal complement components" as a Disease Class span since it denotes a broad category rather than one named condition.
